summary: The Spirit-wrought turning of the whole person from sin to God, distinct from but inseparable from saving faith
readingInstruction: Read Acts 2:37-41 and 2 Corinthians 7:8-11. Today is a doctrinal pause on repentance, turning from sin to God. Notice what Peter says after his sermon, and how Paul distinguishes two kinds of grief.
settingTheScene: Peter has just preached the first Christian sermon, and the crowd has been told that they crucified the Messiah. Their question is the most important question: what shall we do? Peter’s answer begins with repentance. In 2 Corinthians, Paul writes to a church he had grieved with a stern letter, and he rejoices at the result, not because they were hurt, but because the hurt led to repentance.
observation: “Now when they heard this they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, Brothers, what shall we do?” (Acts 2:37).
“Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38).
“For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself” (Acts 2:39).
“So those who received his word were baptized, and there were added that day about three thousand souls” (Acts 2:41).
“As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting” (2 Corinthians 7:9).
“For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret” (2 Corinthians 7:10).
“For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you” (2 Corinthians 7:11).
doctrinalFocus: Repentance is a change of mind and heart about sin and God that results in a change of direction. It includes three elements: recognizing sin for what it is, being sorry for it (not just for its consequences but because it offends God), and turning from it to God, with a purpose to obey. Repentance and faith are two sides of one turning: repentance turns from sin and faith turns to Christ. Jesus began his ministry by calling for both (Mark 1:15). Repentance is a gift of God (Acts 11:18, 2 Timothy 2:25), not a work that earns forgiveness, and it is a lifelong habit, not a one-time act. As Luther put it, the whole life of believers should be repentance. The Bible distinguishes godly grief from worldly grief. Worldly grief is sorrow over being caught or over the damage done to oneself. It can lead to bitterness or despair, as with Judas. Godly grief is sorrow over having sinned against God, and it moves us toward him. It leads to confession, change, and joy. Repentance does not bring forgiveness by its own merit. Forgiveness is on the basis of Christ’s death, received by faith. But there is no saving faith without repentance.
interpretation:
The crowd at Pentecost is “cut to the heart.” The Spirit has convicted them, as Jesus promised. They do not argue or defend themselves. They ask, “What shall we do?” Peter replies, “Repent and be baptized.” Repentance is first. It involves a change of mind about who Jesus is: the one they crucified is Lord and Christ. It involves a change of heart toward sin. Then comes baptism, the outward sign of entering the Christian community and being cleansed. The promise is the forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit. And the promise is for them, for their children, and for all who are far off, whom the Lord calls. Peter urges, “Save yourselves from this crooked generation.” About three thousand were added that day.

Paul’s letter to the Corinthians draws a vital distinction. Earlier he had sent a painful letter. He is glad, not because it hurt them, but because their pain led somewhere. “Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.” Compare Peter, who wept bitterly and was restored, with Judas, who was remorseful but went away and hanged himself. Both felt sorrow. Peter’s sorrow brought him back to Christ. Judas’s sorrow turned inward and ended in despair.

Then Paul lists the fruit of true repentance: earnestness, eagerness to clear themselves, indignation, fear, longing, zeal, and a readiness to see justice done. Repentance is not just a feeling. It makes a difference in how we live. A genuinely repentant person wants to make things right.

For the new believer, repentance can feel frightening, as though God is looking for a reason to condemn. In fact, repentance is a gift. God leads us to it by his kindness (Romans 2:4). When you see your sin, it is the Spirit at work. And the way to the Father is always open: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
connection: Mark 1:15 and Luke 24:47 call for repentance. Psalm 51 is David’s great prayer of repentance. Joel 2:12-13 calls for returning to the LORD with the whole heart. Luke 15:17-24 is the prodigal’s repentance. Matthew 26:75 and 27:3-5 contrast Peter and Judas. Romans 2:4 says God’s kindness leads to repentance. 1 John 1:9 promises forgiveness. Revelation 2:5 calls churches to repent.
application:
Pray Psalm 51 slowly, and name any sin you need to turn from.

Ask yourself: is my grief over sin godly or worldly? Does it move me toward God or away?

Make a concrete change this week as the fruit of repentance, such as an apology, a restitution, or a broken habit.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the gift of repentance.
Ask him to give you godly grief that leads to life.
Confess a sin and turn from it, in your own words.
